overview.text: Ra (also called Re) was a major ancient Egyptian sun god, connected with creation, kingship and renewal. Egyptians pictured the sun’s daily course as a voyage: Ra crossed the sky in a solar boat and entered the underworld at night, with the journey’s return marking the sun’s rebirth. In Egyptian religious accounts, the serpent Apep (also called Apophis) threatened the boat and the sunrise; gods aboard defended Ra. This story made Ra’s voyage more than a description of the sky: it expressed the continuing contest between order and chaos. Ra is often shown as a falcon-headed man wearing a sun disk, though Egyptian beliefs and portrayals changed over time.

key_facts.text: Ra and Re are alternate spellings of the sun god’s name.
Ra was associated with creation and kingship, as well as the sun; by Egypt’s Fifth Dynasty he had become a major deity.
A common image shows Ra as a man with a hawk’s head and a sun disk encircled by a cobra.
The solar voyage was imagined to continue through the underworld at night, with Ra returning for a new day.
Apep, also known as Apophis, was the serpent enemy who attacked Ra’s boat in the underworld; Egyptian religious stories describe the gods defending it.
